title: Hilbert's 17th, Constructively: An Explicit Rational SOS Certificate for the Motzkin Polynomial
description: Hilbert's 17th problem asks whether every nonnegative real polynomial is a sum of squares of rational functions; Artin's affirmative answer is necessarily axiomatized in the parent entry (artin_hilbert17), and the companion fact that the Motzkin polynomial M = x⁴y² + x²y⁴ − 3x²y² + 1 is not a sum of squares of polynomials is also carried as an axiom. What was missing is the explicit positive witness: a fully machine-checked certificate that Motzkin IS a sum of squares of rational functions. This entry supplies it, with 0 axioms. The heart is one integer-coefficient polynomial identity (an SOS Positivstellensatz certificate): (4 + 4x² + 4y²)·M = (2xy − x³y − xy³)² (three copies) + (x³y − xy³)² + (2x − 2xy²)² + (2y − 2x²y)² + (2 − 2x²y²)², closed by ring. The multiplier 4 + 4x² + 4y² = 2² + (2x)² + (2y)² is itself a sum of squares, so dividing through in the field of rational functions ℝ(x,y) and using that a product of two sums of squares is a sum of squares yields M = Σ (rational function)² — Artin's theorem made constructive for the canonical example. The certificate was found by solving the associated semidefinite Gram-matrix feasibility problem: Motzkin sits on the boundary of the SOS cone, and the rational boundary Gram matrix factors into the five squares above.

overview.historicalContext: Hilbert's 17th problem (1900) asked whether every real polynomial that is nonnegative everywhere can be written as a sum of squares of rational functions. Emil Artin answered yes in 1927 (Über die Zerlegung definiter Funktionen in Quadrate), using the theory of formally real / real-closed fields. The necessity of rational functions — rather than polynomials — is shown by explicit counterexamples; the canonical one is the Motzkin polynomial $M(x,y) = x^4y^2 + x^2y^4 - 3x^2y^2 + 1$, which is nonnegative (by AM–GM) yet is provably not a sum of squares of polynomials. The parent gallery entry hilbert-17 states Artin's theorem and the Motzkin counterexample but must carry both as axioms, since the general proof needs real-closed-field model theory. This entry supplies the missing positive, constructive content for the canonical example.
overview.problemStatement: Exhibit and machine-check an explicit witness that the Motzkin polynomial $M = x^4y^2 + x^2y^4 - 3x^2y^2 + 1$ is a sum of squares of rational functions in $\mathbb{R}(x,y)$, i.e. $M = \sum_i g_i^2$ with each $g_i \in \mathbb{R}(x,y)$, with $0$ axioms. This is Artin's theorem made constructive for the instance that is known to fail polynomial SOS, thereby replacing the parent entry's existence axiom $\texttt{artin\_hilbert17}$ for this $M$.
overview.proofStrategy: The core is a single integer-coefficient SOS Positivstellensatz certificate, closed entirely by $\texttt{ring}$: the multiplier $4 + 4x^2 + 4y^2$ times $M$ equals a sum of seven polynomial squares, $(2xy - x^3y - xy^3)^2$ (three copies) $+ (x^3y - xy^3)^2 + (2x - 2xy^2)^2 + (2y - 2x^2y)^2 + (2 - 2x^2y^2)^2$. The multiplier itself is a sum of squares, $4 + 4x^2 + 4y^2 = 2^2 + (2x)^2 + (2y)^2$. Working in the fraction field $\mathbb{R}(x,y) = \mathrm{FractionRing}\,\mathbb{R}[x,y]$, one shows the multiplier is nonzero (its constant term is $4$, via evaluation at $0$) and its image in $\mathbb{R}(x,y)$ is nonzero (using $\texttt{IsFractionRing.injective}$). Then, using that a product of two sums of squares is a sum of squares — $(\sum a_i^2)(\sum b_j^2) = \sum_{i,j}(a_ib_j)^2$ — the $7$-square certificate for $(\text{multiplier})\cdot M$ and the $3$-square certificate for the multiplier combine into a $21$-term polynomial identity $\sum_{i<7,j<3}(q_i d_j)^2 = (\text{multiplier}\cdot M)\cdot\text{multiplier}$. Dividing through by $\text{multiplier}^2$ in the field and reindexing $\mathrm{Fin}\,7 \times \mathrm{Fin}\,3 \simeq \mathrm{Fin}\,21$ yields $M = \sum_{i,j}(q_i d_j / (4+4x^2+4y^2))^2$, a sum of $21$ squares of rational functions. The certificate was discovered by solving the associated semidefinite Gram-matrix feasibility problem numerically (alternating projection onto the affine constraint set and the PSD cone) and reading off the rational boundary Gram factorization.
keyInsights: Rational functions are genuinely necessary: the Motzkin polynomial is nonnegative everywhere yet is not a sum of squares of polynomials, so a polynomial SOS witness cannot exist — only the rational-function representation succeeds, which is exactly what makes Hilbert's 17th problem deeper than the polynomial case.

The whole construction reduces to one integer-coefficient polynomial identity that Lean closes by $\texttt{ring}$: $(4+4x^2+4y^2)\cdot M = 3G_0^2 + G_1^2 + G_2^2 + G_3^2 + G_4^2$. Because the identity is over a known finite set of monomials with integer coefficients, no heavy machinery is needed — verification is purely algebraic.

The auxiliary multiplier must itself be a sum of squares for the argument to work: $4 + 4x^2 + 4y^2 = 2^2 + (2x)^2 + (2y)^2$. Combined with the product-of-SOS-is-SOS identity, this is precisely what converts the polynomial certificate $(\text{multiplier})\cdot M = \text{SOS}$ into a genuine rational-function SOS for $M$ after dividing by the multiplier.

Division by the multiplier is legitimized formally: the multiplier is nonzero in $\mathbb{R}[x,y]$ (its evaluation at $0$ is the constant term $4 \neq 0$), and $\texttt{IsFractionRing.injective}$ lifts this to a nonzero image in $\mathbb{R}(x,y)$, so the field division step is sound rather than assumed.

Motzkin sits on the boundary of the SOS cone, so the certificate was not guessed but computed: solving the semidefinite Gram-matrix feasibility problem (SOS/SDP duality) produces the rational boundary Gram matrix, which factors into the five explicit squares — demonstrating the SDP-to-formal-proof pipeline of solve numerically, read off a rational Gram factorization, then discharge the resulting identity with $\texttt{ring}$.

The result is $0$-axiom: $\#\texttt{print axioms}$ on $\texttt{motzkin\_isSOS\_ratFunc}$ reports only $\texttt{propext}$, $\texttt{Classical.choice}$, $\texttt{Quot.sound}$ — no $\texttt{sorryAx}$ and no $\texttt{native\_decide}$/$\texttt{Lean.ofReduceBool}$ — so it replaces the parent's existence axiom $\texttt{artin\_hilbert17}$ for this $M$ with a fully machine-checked witness. The $21 = 7\times 3$ squares are un-optimized; the true minimum (a Pfister-type bound) is smaller.

conclusion.summary: A 177-line, 0-sorry, 0-axiom formalization giving an explicit, machine-checked rational sum-of-squares certificate for the Motzkin polynomial: the constructive, positive side of Hilbert's 17th problem for the canonical example, complementing the parent's axiomatized general Artin theorem.
conclusion.implications: Where the parent only asserts existence of a rational SOS (artin_hilbert17 as an axiom), this entry exhibits one for Motzkin and verifies it with 0 axioms. It also demonstrates the Gram-matrix / SDP route to SOS certificates inside a formal proof: solve the SDP numerically, read off the rational boundary Gram factorization, and discharge the resulting polynomial identity with ring.
openQuestions: Minimize the number of rational-function squares: the construction uses 21 = 7×3; the true minimum (Pfister-type bound) for Motzkin over ℝ(x,y) is smaller and could be certified directly.
Discharge the companion axiom motzkin_not_sos_polynomial_aux (Motzkin is not a polynomial SOS) by the coefficient/degree argument, closing the negative side as well.
Generalize the SDP-certificate pipeline to the Robinson form (robinson_not_sos_aux) and other extremal PSD polynomials in the parent file.

sections.title: Header: A Constructive SOS Certificate for the Motzkin Polynomial
sections.summary: States the gap this file fills — the parent Hilbert-17 entry's Artin theorem (every nonnegative real polynomial is a sum of squares of rational functions) is necessarily axiomatized, and even the companion fact that the Motzkin polynomial M(x,y) = x⁴y²+x²y⁴−3x²y²+1 is not a sum of squares of polynomials is carried as an axiom; missing was an explicit, machine-checked witness that Motzkin is a sum of squares of rational functions. This file supplies exactly that with 0 axioms, via the integer Positivstellensatz certificate (4+4x²+4y²)·M = five explicit squares, closed by ring, then dividing by the sum-of-squares multiplier 4+4x²+4y² = 2²+(2x)²+(2y)² in the field of rational functions — replacing Hilbert's 17th problem's abstract existence axiom with a concrete certificate for this canonical example.
sections.mathContext: $(4+4x^2+4y^2)\cdot M(x,y) = (2xy-x^3y-xy^3)^2{\times}3 + (x^3y-xy^3)^2 + (2x-2xy^2)^2 + (2y-2x^2y)^2 + (2-2x^2y^2)^2$, an integer SOS certificate closed by \texttt{ring}.

sections.title: Motzkin, the multiplier, and the SOS predicates
sections.summary: motzkin = x⁴y² + x²y⁴ − 3x²y² + 1 (defined identically to the parent entry); multiplier = 4 + 4x² + 4y²; the polynomial- and rational-function- sum-of-squares predicates IsSumOfSquaresMv and IsSumOfSquaresRF over ℝ(x,y) = FractionRing ℝ[x,y]; and the integer-coefficient generators G0…G4 and the witness vectors qv (seven roots) and dv (three roots of the multiplier).

sections.title: The polynomial SOS certificate
sections.summary: multiplier_mul_motzkin_eq is the integer-coefficient identity (4+4x²+4y²)·M = 3G0² + G1² + G2² + G3² + G4², closed by ring; motzkin_mul_isSumOfSquares packages it as IsSumOfSquaresMv, and multiplier_isSumOfSquares shows the multiplier is 2²+(2x)²+(2y)².

sections.title: The Certificate Proves Nonnegativity (Positivstellensatz Payoff)
sections.summary: multiplier_eval_pos: the strictly positive multiplier 4 + 4x² + 4y² ≥ 4 > 0 never vanishes at a real point; motzkin_eval_nonneg then evaluates the certificate multiplier·M = Σ Gᵢ² at any v, so multiplier(v)·M(v) = Σ Gᵢ(v)² ≥ 0 with multiplier(v) > 0 forces M(v) ≥ 0. This recovers Motzkin nonnegativity as a corollary of the exhibited SOS Positivstellensatz certificate — the logical payoff of having the certificate, independent of the direct AM–GM route.

sections.title: Artin for Motzkin, Constructively (Rational-Function Corollary)
sections.summary: multiplier_ne_zero / toRF_multiplier_ne_zero validate division by the multiplier in ℝ(x,y) = FractionRing ℝ[x,y]; product_identity is the 21-term polynomial identity Σ(qᵢdⱼ)² = (multiplier·M)·multiplier; motzkin_isSOS_ratFunc divides through and reindexes Fin 7 × Fin 3 ≃ Fin 21 to conclude M = Σ (qᵢdⱼ/multiplier)², a sum of squares of rational functions — the constructive Artin representation realising Hilbert's 17th problem for Motzkin.
